t: “Celts” was a Greek name for peoples of the European interior; today it is used above all for speakers of Celtic languages, who in the Iron Age lived from Iberia and Ireland to the Danube.
Archaeologists associate them with the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures, known for salt mines, rich princely burials, hillforts, the walled towns called oppida and a flowing, abstract art.
Celtic war bands sacked Rome and attacked Delphi, but Rome conquered most Celtic lands from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE; the languages survive in Ireland, Scotland, Wales and Brittany.
dyk: The Greek bronze krater, a vessel for mixing wine, found in a princely grave at Vix in Burgundy stands 1.64 metres high, weighs 208.6 kilograms and holds about 1,100 litres: the largest Greek bronze vessel known.
ev: Iron working spreads in central Europe and the Hallstatt culture begins
Greeks from Phocaea found Massalia; Greek wine and bronzes reach the Hallstatt princes
The La Tène culture and its art style emerge between Champagne and Bohemia
Gauls under Brennus rout the Romans at the Allia and sack Rome
A Celtic army attacks Delphi; three tribes cross into Asia Minor and settle in Galatia
Rome destroys a Gallic army at Telamon and goes on to conquer Cisalpine Gaul
Julius Caesar conquers Gaul; Vercingetorix surrenders at Alesia in 52 BCE
Rome conquers most of Britain, crushing Boudica’s revolt and winning at Mons Graupius

f.homeland: Central and western Europe: present-day France, Belgium, Switzerland, southern Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic, northern Italy, Spain, Portugal, Britain and Ireland, with offshoots on the middle Danube, in the Balkans and in central Anatolia (Galatia)
f.period: The Hallstatt culture c. 800–450 BCE and the La Tène culture from c. 450 BCE to the Roman conquest (Gaul 58–50 BCE, most of Britain 43–84 CE); Ireland was never conquered, and Celtic languages live on
f.known: The salt mines and princely burials of the Hallstatt world; La Tène art; hillforts and the towns called oppida; the druids; the sack of Rome c. 390 BCE and the resistance of Vercingetorix and Boudica
f.sources: Greek and Roman writers (Hecataeus, Herodotus, Polybius, Posidonius through Diodorus and Strabo, Caesar, Tacitus); inscriptions in Lepontic, Celtiberian and Gaulish; coins; excavated sites such as Hallstatt, La Tène, Hochdorf, Vix, Manching and Bibracte; medieval Irish and Welsh literature
